title: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
author: Ryan Devereaux
content:
Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to
offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border
wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the
bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places
of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors.

“People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said.

Fifteen days later, her fears were realized.

ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ
Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors.

The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park
Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University
of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human
and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said.

The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps
agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American
remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that
contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted.

“The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and
traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently
to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return
of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural
practices.”

Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the
Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe,
and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what
to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly
unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will
disturb more sites.

“​​Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re
going to find remains wherever they dig.”

![An Indigenous woman who has long gray hair and wears a sun hat stands
amongst several saguaro cactuses in a desert
landscape.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/220212_EM_0244.jpg?w=2560)Hia-Ced O’odham elder
Lorraine Eiler stands in the shade of a giant saguaro cactus in Organ Pipe
National Monument in 2022. Roberto “Bear” Guerra

Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of
vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned
staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting
to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told
the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a
saguaro cactus that was still standing.

In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was
made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no
other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this
location to date.”

The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security
and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall
contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as
the [Las Playas Intaglio](https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-
environment/2026/04/30/border-wall-damage-indigenous-arizona/), that was
believed to be at [least
6,500](https://mydigitalpublication.com/publication/?i=870459&p=30&view=issueViewer)
years old. (CBP [said the incident was
accidental](https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-
environment/2026/04/30/border-wall-damage-indigenous-arizona/).)

Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of
a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The
tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no
trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica
recently reported, DHS has responded by [deploying masked federal agents as
escorts for its work crews](https://www.propublica.org/article/tohono-oodham-
nation-arizona-border-wall) and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal
members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the
reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors
on the Southwest border.”

Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park
service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it
was necessary.

“When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where
there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural
importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a
statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members
of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members —
whose remains are being desecrated.”

U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the
August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their
warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating
consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the
destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months,
those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they
feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.”

* * *

James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the
University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the
field.

While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without
park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains
were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent
with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.

Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently
uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained,
and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal
descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the
land.”

“Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30
calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal
representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the
remains.”

![Heavy construction equipment works next to the existing border wall in a
desert landscape, with a dirt access road, tall light poles, saguaro cactuses
and distant mountains visible through the haze of dust kicked up by the large
vehicles.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/260831_Watts-
Quitobaquito-2-1_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Workers clear desert
flora to make way for construction of a double border wall in Organ Pipe
National Monument. Anna Watts

* * *

In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the
inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some
regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary
powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall
construction in the borderlands.

Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID
Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any
law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS
has [invoked its powers](https://u.osu.edu/madsen.34/dhs-waivers/) 66 times,
with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two
administrations.

When DHS uses this authority, it typically waives dozens of laws at a time.
That was the case in 2019 when the department set its sights on Organ Pipe. [A
waiver](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/05/15/2019-10079/determination-
pursuant-to-section-102-of-the-illegal-immigration-reform-and-immigrant-
responsibility) issued by then-acting Secretary Kevin K. McAleenan set aside
more than 40 of the nation’s most stringent environmental and cultural
resource protection laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the
Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act and others. Also on that list was
the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, the landmark 1990
law that acknowledged [the nation’s long history of desecrating Native
American burials](https://www.propublica.org/article/repatriation-nagpra-
museums-human-remains) and required that ancestral remains and cultural
objects be returned to tribes.

In an [internal 2019 report](https://games-
cdn.washingtonpost.com/notes/prod/default/documents/cbd7ef6a-3b5b-4608-9913-4d488464823b/note/7a429f63-9e46-41fa-
afeb-c8e238fcd8bb.pdf)[
obtained](https://www.washingtonpost.com/immigration/border-fence-
construction-could-destroy-archaeological-sites-national-park-service-
finds/2019/09/17/35338b18-d64b-11e9-9343-40db57cf6abd_story.html) by The
Washington Post, park service officials identified nearly two dozen
archaeological sites in Organ Pipe as at risk of damage or total destruction
by government contractors.

Of particular significance is a desert oasis known as Quitobaquito Springs.
Less than 200 feet from the international border, the springs provide one of
the only reliable sources of groundwater and shade for miles around, and they
were a longtime gathering place, grazing site and home for O’odham families.

“Archaeological evidence of human presence at Quitobaquito extends back
thousands of years, at least to Archaic times,” the survey found, adding that
the springs represent the “only known Hia C-ed O’odham village site in the
United States.”

A [park service
report](https://capla.arizona.edu/sites/default/files/2024-06/Quitobaquito%20Cultural%20Landscape%20Report%20FINAL%201-11-24.pdf)
in 2024 noted that a cemetery at Quitobaquito holds the remains of at least
two families, including Eiler’s, and 34 graves. Throughout the region,
[remains of 5,500 ancestors](https://projects.propublica.org/repatriation-
nagpra-database/tribe/tohono-oodham-nation-arizona/) that were displaced have
been made available for return to the Tohono O’odham Nation, according to
[ProPublica’s NAGPRA database](https://projects.propublica.org/repatriation-
nagpra-database/).

“This sort of incident has happened numerous times across our homeland, and
it’s always alarming to hear about a case from an O’odham point of view,” said
David Martínez, a professor of American Indian and transborder studies at the
University of Arizona and a member of the Hia-Ced O’odham and Akimel O’odham
tribes, as well as the Gila River Indian Community.

“Those remains shouldn’t have been disturbed in the first place,” he said.
“While there are protocols existing today to properly care for these remains,
ultimately, whatever either the government or the corporate world is pursuing
to build, we know that at some juncture that construction will continue, and
it always leaves us feeling, I think, a little hollow.”

Today, Quitobaquito lies in the shadow of the border wall erected during
Trump’s first term. Its construction required [detonating
explosives](https://theintercept.com/2020/02/06/border-wall-construction-
organ-pipe/) in the national monument, blasting apart an area called Monument
Hill and outraging tribal leaders. According to Eiler, the remains recovered
in September were not found at the springs, though government work crews are
working in close proximity to the site.

This year, DHS hired Sundt Construction, an Arizona-based company, to build a
second wall in the monument. The [$443 million
contract](https://www.usaspending.gov/award/CONT_AWD_70B01C26F00000403_7014_70B01C26D00000009_7014)
was finalized in May. (Sundt directed questions concerning the discovery of
human remains on its job site to CBP.)

According to CBP, the 2019 waiver for Organ Pipe is still in effect, years
after completion of the project that prompted it. A [second
waiver](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/11/19/2025-20292/determination-
pursuant-to-section-102-of-the-illegal-immigration-reform-and-immigrant-
responsibility), exempting DHS from many of the same laws and applying to the
national monument as well as a wildlife refuge to the west, was issued by
Homeland Security’s then-Secretary Kristi Noem last year.

“Unfortunately, there is no end date to the effectiveness of the waivers,”
said Dinah Bear, a Tucson-based lawyer who served for 25 years as a senior
attorney in the White House’s Council on Environmental Quality under both
Democratic and Republican administrations. What’s more, she added, “there’s
nothing in the statutory language that ties the waivers to a particular
project.”

The Department of Homeland Security’s waiver powers have been central to a
high-profile legal fight over the department’s efforts to build a border wall
through Big Bend National Park in West Texas, with a federal judge overseeing
the case recently ordering [a temporary halt](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2026/oct/02/big-bend-national-park-border-wall-halt) to the project.

Borderlands advocates in Arizona are hoping for similar interventions. In
Congress, Grijalva is preparing legislation to void existing waivers that have
allowed DHS to disregard laws designed to protect tribal sovereignty, sacred
sites and environmentally sensitive lands.

In the meantime, construction on the border continues. For Eiler, it’s not
just the destruction in Organ Pipe that’s troubling. She sees the disturbance
of tribal graves resulting from wall construction as reflective of a wider
pattern of destruction across the border.

“It’s sad because it’s not only happening down there,” she said. “It’s
happening all over the United States, and nobody’s saying much about it.”
